title: Dangerous, Dirty, Violent & Young, A Fugitive Family in the Revolutionary Underground
author: Ed Rampell
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screen-
Shot-2026-07-21-at-10.57.24-AM-680x531.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/22/dangerous-
dirty-violent-young-a-fugitive-family-in-the-revolutionary-underground/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screen-
Shot-2026-07-21-at-10.57.24-AM-680x531.png)

Bernardine Dohrn (left), Bill Ayers (right), Zayd Ayers Dohrn (center) with
his brother in Harlem, after a long drive through the underground in 1980.
(Courtesy of Peter Clapp)

Zayd Ayers Dohrn has quite a story to tell, and fortunately for readers, he is
a stellar storyteller. A prize-winning playwright, Zayd may hold the title of
the Daniel Hale Williams Professor and Director of the MFA in Writing for the
Screen + Stage at Northwestern University, but, as America commemorates the
250th anniversary of its Revolution, Zayd’s personal saga calls to mind the
patriot Nathan Hale, that Continental Army soldier and undercover agent famed
for saying: “I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country.”

Almost 200 years later, that same revolutionary spirit animated Zayd’s
parents, who were combatants in another insurrectionist force taking up arms
to overthrow the government – but instead of being “Continental,” it was an
underground army of would-be urban guerrillas. By 1969, the Weathermen were
struggling to “off the pigs” “by any means necessary,” deploying stridently
militant opposition against the ruling class with what anarchists called “the
propaganda of the deed,” blowing up targets symbolic of the powers-that-be,
primarily to protest the Vietnam War and racism.

In his alternately rip-roaring and introspective nonfiction narrative,
_Dangerous, Dirty, Violent & Young, A Fugitive Family in the Revolutionary
Underground _(W.W. Norton), about growing up radical with his mom and dad,
Zayd writes: “by 1970, when she was only twenty-eight years old, Bernardine
[Dohrn]… my mother became only the fourth woman in history on the FBI’s Ten
Most Wanted list.” The first female on that infamous “top ten list” was a
kidnapper, while the second was a murderer; but as Zayd writes about
Bernardine, “The CIA said she was ‘the most rabid female radical in the
country.’ FBI director J. Edgar Hoover called her ‘the most dangerous woman in
America.’” (Bernardine, who according to her most wanted poster was charged
with “violation of Federal Antiriot Laws and conspiracy,” actually had much
more in common with the third woman ever inducted onto the FBI’s top ten list:
Angela Davis. But that’s another story.)

Zayd’s dad, Bill Ayers, was another Weather warrior who attained national
notoriety. In 1975 Bill was depicted by none other than Henry Winkler (who
played Fonzie in the popular 1970s sitcom _Happy Days_) in the made-for-TV
movie _Katherine_ , arguably the best fiction film ever made about the white
New Left, written/directed by Jeremy Kagan (who went on to make the 1987 HBO
movie _Conspiracy: The Trial of the Chicago 8_). In _Katherine_ , Sissy Spacek
portrayed a character largely based on Diana Oughton, one of the Weathermen
who died March 6, 1970 in a Manhattan townhouse, when bombs being made there
accidentally exploded. Bill had been one of Oughton’s lovers, and Bob Kline,
the composite character Winkler played in Katherine, was based in part on him.
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screen-
Shot-2026-07-21-at-10.55.32-AM-680x1026.png)](https://bookshop.org/a/81622/9781324089315)

**The Only Solution is Revolution**

Kagan’s surprisingly sympathetic movie convincingly dramatized how middle-
class white youths who sought to peacefully change the system through legal
means were increasingly radicalized by an intransigent system that waged war
on Vietnam abroad and perpetrated racism domestically. Unable to end the war
and racial injustice nonviolently and legally, _Katherine’s_ increasingly
enraged and engaged characters inexorably move towards armed struggle against
the state. In his 427-page _Dangerous, Dirty, Violent & Young, _Zayd provides
an eyewitness, detailed account of why the real-life Bill and Bernardine
turned their backs on the white-skin, middle-to-upper-class privilege they
were born into to co-found a clandestine, “vanguard” organization that
declared war on the U.S. government.

After Oughton’s death, Bill and Bernardine became partners and eventually
married. Zayd movingly relates what it was like growing up the son of a sort
of ultraleft version of Bonnie and Clyde, on the lam from the FBI, living
clandestinely and coming of age in, as his subtitle puts it, _A Fugitive
Family in the Revolutionary Underground_. Zayd spins an amazing yarn about the
Weathermen trying to “bring the war home,” with the so-called “Days of Rage”
street fighting against the Chicago Police Department; bombings at police
stations, the Pentagon, the State Department, the Capitol Building (decades
before the Jan. 6, 2021 riot there), etc.; bank robberies; armored car heists;
prison breakouts, including of LSD guru Timothy Leary and Black Liberation
Army leader Assata Shakur; and much more.

But this book, which often reads like a novel, proving the old cliché that
“truth is stranger than fiction” can be true, is interwoven with Zayd’s
insightful, poignant ruminations about the cost his parents’ and their
comrades’ extremism exacted on their children who were born into and reared in
the underground.

Even more importantly, in retrospect, _Dangerous, Dirty, Violent & Young
_raises major questions about the role the Weathermen played in the movement
and the terrorist tactics they used. In 1968, Bernardine was elected one of
the three national leaders of Students for a Democratic Society. But the
following year, at SDS’s national convention, advocating a more hardline
direct action approach, Bernardine led a walkout, splitting the organization,
which, as Zayd notes, had “350 chapters nationwide,” with “100,000” members
and was America’s “largest student activist group.”

Zayd also writes that the FBI closely monitored SDS, and one can’t help but
wonder whether SDS’ so-called “action faction” unwittingly (and perhaps egged
on by provocateurs?) played into the hands of the FBI’s COINTELPRO
counterintelligence, counterinsurgency program that surveilled, infiltrated,
and disrupted the New Left. Frustrated by the failure of peaceful civil
disobedience, lawful demonstrations and other activities to end the Vietnam
War and racism (after all, the apostle of nonviolence, Dr. King, had been
assassinated), the Weathermen resorted to extralegal means of violent armed
resistance.

But this divided the antiwar and civil rights movements, which advocated
nonviolent methods of protest. Street fighting, bombings, and the like also
could be used to discredit the mass movement to end the war in Vietnam, which
was, of course, dedicated to giving peace a chance. Explosions at places such
as police headquarters – even if authorities were notified in advance to
evacuate the premises – also unintentionally gave “law and order” politicians
and authorities the opportunity to crack down on all forms of dissent.

A prominent veteran of the Columbia University protest and co-founder of the
Weathermen, Mark Rudd, rued the role he played in the SDS split. Rudd is
quoted in _Dangerous, Dirty, Violent & Young _as calling his participation in
the walkout “‘the single greatest mistake in my life. … I chose to scuttle
America’s largest radical organization … for a fantasy of revolutionary urban
guerrilla warfare.’”

History will judge whether these faction fights and the Weather Underground’s
extremism played a truly revolutionary or a counterrevolutionary role by
dividing the growing peace movement. How effective were the Weathermen in
advancing their stated causes? Zayd writes about how his parents and a handful
of other zealots became increasingly isolated and extreme, with harrowing
accounts of shootouts and the like, going up against the wall of
“motherfuckers” who were far better armed and trained and greatly outnumbered
them.

**The Song Remains the Same?**

The name of the extremist “vanguard” organization Bernardine co-founded in
1969 was derived from Bob Dylan’s lyrics in “Subterranean Homesick Blues”:
“You don’t need a weatherman, To know which way the wind blows.” And the
Weather Underground fancied themselves to be the song’s “vandals [who] took
the handles” so “The pump don’t work.”

Likewise, the title of Zayd’s gripping chronicle comes from another song,
Jefferson Airplane’s “We Can Be Together,” which a period rock critic called
“a virtual ‘state of the union’ address for the counterculture of the late
’60s.” According to the author, his book’s name “comes from a Jefferson
Airplane lyric. Jefferson Airplane was one of the musical groups that actually
gave money to the underground. They were counterculture rock stars and they
donated money to keep the underground alive. It’s a tribute to them and to
that connection. That particular lyric goes:

_“We are all outlaws in the eyes of America_  
_[In order to survive, we steal, cheat, lie, forge, fuck, hide and deal]_  
_We are obscene, lawless, hideous, dangerous, dirty, violent_  
_And young.”_

Zayd added: “It was a way of saying then that anybody who didn’t fit into the
consensus of American mainstream culture – whether you were a woman or queer
or Black – you were an outlaw, didn’t belong in some way, that you were
underground. That lyric became a touchstone for my parents and their friends,
they used to say: ‘We are all outlaws in the eyes of America.’ That lyric said
something about who they were then and who they were trying to be.”

_Dangerous, Dirty, Violent & Young _recounts what happened to Bernardine Dohrn
and Bill Ayers once they emerged from about a decade of living underground.
Years after fading into obscurity as mostly forgotten aging heroes/villains
(take your pick) of the New Left, the onetime outlaws were thrust back into
the limelight by both Sen. Hillary Clinton and Republican V.P. candidate Sarah
Palin during the 2008 presidential race. As Zayd writes, when Alaska’s
governor accused the Democratic contender of being “a person who sees America
as imperfect enough to pal around with [domestic] terrorists who targeted
their own country,” those “pals” Palin was referring to were Bill and
Bernardine, because of “the fact that Obama had held one of his early
fundraisers in our Chicago living room, and he and my dad had served on the
board of a nonprofit together.” Zayd quotes David Axelrod, the chief
strategist to Barack Obama’s campaign, as telling him: “They wanted to turn
him into a scary, radical Black man. And so Bernardine Dohrn, Bill Ayers,
famous names from the radical past, were resurfaced for that purpose.”

This is just one of the many tales in an exciting book jam-packed with
anecdotes that makes _Dangerous, Dirty, Violent & Young_ a fascinating, great
read. Indeed, this insider account is a must-read for aficionados of New Left
history, with lots of text about the Panther 21, the Black Liberation Army and
political prisoner Assata Shakur, who eventually escaped from prison to live
in exile in Cuba. Other legendary figures of the Left also turn up in this
harrowing saga, including the great attorney Leonard Boudin, who represented
Paul Robeson, Daniel Ellsberg and Dr. Spock, as well as Leonard’s daughter
Kathy Boudin, who survived the townhouse explosion that killed Oughton but
went on to be imprisoned for her role in the BLA’s bloody Brink’s armored car
robbery in 1981. While she served hard time for about 23 years, Bill and
Bernardine adopted their toddler, Chesa Boudin, who went on to be elected San
Francisco’s District Attorney, but was recalled in 2022.

As we live in another era of political violence, _Dangerous, Dirty, Violent &
Young _provides insight and context for the efficacy and justification – or
lack of – for extremist direct action and propaganda of the deed. It is also a
thoughtful meditation on how the choices of ideologically motivated parents
impact their children who did not choose to be born into and raised in a life
of struggle. Like the Revolution, the generation gap is permanent.

One can almost imagine Zayd arguing with his mother and father, who try to
shut him down, as he replies: “But you always taught me to disobey authority!”
To which Bill and Bernardine respond: “Yes, but we meant Nixon – not us!”
